lead: A ferromagnet does not retrace its magnetization curve when the applied field is removed. The B-H plot traces a closed loop called the hysteresis loop. Its area is the energy lost as heat per unit volume per cycle. Soft magnetic materials have narrow loops, low coercivity and small loss; they go into transformer cores and inductors. Hard magnetic materials have wide loops, high coercivity and high retentivity; they become permanent magnets. The same loop explains why a transformer core heats up and why a fridge magnet keeps its field.
prereq: You need: Chapter 7.7 on domains and ferromagnetism.

blocks.text: Two fields describe a magnetic material. The magnetic field strength H is set by currents and is measured in ampere per metre (A/m). The magnetic flux density B is the resulting field inside the material and is measured in tesla (T). For a linear material B = μ0 μr H, where μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m is the vacuum permeability and μr is the relative permeability. For a ferromagnet the relation is not linear and not single-valued.

Start with an unmagnetized sample and raise H. B rises steeply, then bends over and saturates at B<sub>s</sub>. Domains that already point along H grow, and domains that oppose H shrink or rotate. At high H all domains are aligned and further increase of H gives only the small slope μ0.

Now reduce H to zero. B does not return to zero. The value left at H = 0 is the retentivity B_r. Reverse H until B becomes zero; the magnitude of that reverse field is the coercivity H_c. Continue to negative saturation and back, and the path closes into a loop. Domain wall motion is easy at first and reversible; pinning at defects makes part of the motion irreversible, and that irreversibility opens the loop.

The area of the closed B-H loop is the work done by the source on unit volume of material in one cycle. Write it as the formula below. W_h is the hysteresis loss per unit volume per cycle, in joule per cubic metre (J/m³); H is in A/m; B is in T; the integral goes once around the loop. The unit check is (A/m) × T = (A/m) × (N/(A·m)) = N/m² = J/m³.

blocks.where: W_h is the hysteresis energy loss per unit volume per cycle (J/m³); H is the magnetic field strength (A/m); B is the magnetic flux density (T); the integral is taken once around the closed B-H loop.

blocks.text: A core of volume V taken through the loop f times per second loses hysteresis power P_h = W_h V f. V is in cubic metres (m³) and f is in hertz (Hz = cycles per second). The loss rises linearly with frequency for a fixed loop. It also depends on the peak flux density B<sub>m</sub>, because a larger B<sub>m</sub> sweeps a larger loop.

Eddy currents give a second loss. Changing B induces currents inside the core, and their Joule heating adds to the hysteresis heat. Eddy-current loss grows roughly as f² and is reduced by making the core from thin, insulated laminated sheets or by using a high-resistivity ferrite. Lamination does not reduce hysteresis loss; that needs a soft material with a narrow loop.

A soft magnetic material has a narrow loop, low coercivity H_c, high relative permeability μr and small hysteresis loss per cycle. It is easy to magnetize and easy to demagnetize. Silicon steel, soft ferrites and permalloy are common. Transformer cores, inductors, chokes and the magnetic cores of high-frequency switching supplies use soft materials because the core is taken around its loop many times every second.

A hard magnetic material has a wide loop, high coercivity and high retentivity. It is hard to demagnetize, so it holds a large field after the magnetizing source is removed. Alnico, hard ferrites, samarium-cobalt (SmCo) and neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB) are used. Permanent magnets in motors, loudspeakers, door catches, magnetic separators and small generators use hard materials.

The product B_r H_c, or more strictly the maximum energy product (BH)_max, measures how much magnetic energy a hard magnet can supply in a gap. A large (BH)_max means a smaller magnet for the same job. A soft material with high B<sub>s</sub> but low H_c is not a permanent magnet: it loses its field as soon as the current is switched off. 'Hard' here means magnetically hard, not mechanically hard.

figure.caption: Schematic B-H loops: the soft material has a narrow loop with small coercivity; the hard material has a wide loop with large retentivity and coercivity. The enclosed area is the hysteresis loss per unit volume per cycle.

spec.aria: Schematic B-H loops: the soft loop is narrow and the hard loop is wide; the area enclosed is the hysteresis loss.

examples.question: A transformer core has volume 500 cm³. Its hysteresis loop has area 250 J/m³ per cycle at 50 Hz. Find the hysteresis power loss.
steps: Convert volume: V = 500 cm³ = 500 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 0.0005 m³.
Energy lost per cycle: E = area × V = 250 J/m³ × 0.0005 m³ = 0.125 J.
Cycles per second: f = 50 Hz = 50 s⁻¹.
examples.answer: The hysteresis power loss is 6.25 W.
examples.check:
V_cm3 = 500
V = V_cm3 * 1e-6
w = 250
f = 50
E = w * V
P = E * f
print(V)
print(E)
print(P)

traps: The loop area is energy per unit volume per cycle (J/m³), not power. To get power, multiply by core volume and frequency.
B is in tesla and H is in A/m. Do not add or plot them as if they had the same unit.
Retentivity B_r is the B left at H = 0. Coercivity H_c is the reverse H that makes B = 0. Do not swap the two.
A soft magnet needs low H_c and a narrow loop, not necessarily the highest B<sub>s</sub>. A hard magnet needs high H_c, not high permeability.
Laminations cut eddy-current loss, not hysteresis loss. Hysteresis loss is cut by choosing a magnetically soft material.

quiz.q: Define retentivity B_r and coercivity H_c.
quiz.a: B_r is the flux density remaining at H = 0 after saturation. H_c is the reverse field strength that reduces B to zero.

quiz.q: Why is a soft magnetic material used for a transformer core?
quiz.a: It has a narrow loop and low H_c, so the energy lost per cycle is small. Its high permeability gives a large B for a small H. The core is magnetized and demagnetized 50 times per second, so low loss matters.

quiz.q: A core of volume 200 cm³ has loop area 400 J/m³ per cycle at 50 Hz. Find the hysteresis power loss.
A material has high B_r but low H_c. Is it suitable for a permanent magnet? Explain.
quiz.a: No. High B_r gives a strong field, but low H_c means a small reverse field demagnetizes it. A permanent magnet needs a wide loop with high H_c and large (BH)_max.

quiz.q: State one cause and one reduction method for hysteresis loss and for eddy-current loss.
quiz.a: Hysteresis loss comes from irreversible domain wall motion; reduce it with a soft material of narrow loop. Eddy-current loss comes from induced currents in the core; reduce it with thin insulated laminations or high-resistivity ferrite.

quiz.q: For the same peak flux density, frequency doubles. What happens to hysteresis power and eddy-current power?
quiz.a: Hysteresis power is proportional to f, so it doubles. Eddy-current power is roughly proportional to f², so it becomes four times larger.

quiz.q: Explain why the loop area has units J/m³ and why P = W_h V f gives power.
quiz.a: ∮H dB has units (A/m) × T = (A/m) × (N/(A·m)) = N/m² = J/m³. It is energy per unit volume per cycle. Multiplying by volume V gives energy per cycle; multiplying by f gives energy per second, which is power.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry grades soft magnets by core loss at a stated frequency and flux density, and hard magnets by energy product (BH)_max in kJ/m³. Rare-earth magnets such as NdFeB dominate motors and wind generators, while cheap ferrites dominate high-frequency inductors.
